lead: An array multiplier makes every partial product at the same time. Each bit of the multiplier opens a row of AND gates, and each row is the multiplicand shifted by that bit's place. Full adders then combine the rows at fixed columns, with carries moving diagonally down the array. The answer appears after one long ripple through the diagonals. Braun does this for unsigned numbers. Baugh-Wooley does it for two's complement by inverting the mixed sign partial products and adding two fixed 1 bits. Small embedded multipliers and many hardware interview questions still use these arrays.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.1 for the full adder, and Chapter 4.2 for why saving carries helps when many rows must be added.

sections.h3: Rows of AND gates, added by place value

blocks.text: Write the multiplicand as A = a<sub>n−1</sub>...a<sub>0</sub> and the multiplier as B = b<sub>n−1</sub>...b<sub>0</sub>. Each bit a<sub>i</sub> and b<sub>j</sub> is 0 or 1, and n is the word length. Unsigned multiplication is shift and add. Multiplying by b<sub>j</sub>2<sup>j</sup> either adds A<<j or adds zero. The array does all these additions together.

blocks.where: P is the 2n-bit product; a<sub>i</sub> is bit i of A; b<sub>j</sub> is bit j of B; pp<sub>ij</sub> = a<sub>i</sub>b<sub>j</sub> is one partial product bit; 2<sup>i+j</sup> fixes its column.

blocks.text: A 4×4 array needs 16 AND gates to form pp<sub>00</sub> to pp<sub>33</sub>. It needs 12 full adders to reduce the four rows: n(n−1)=4×3=12. The first row is not added to anything, so it enters the array directly. Carries do not run along a row; they run diagonally into the next row at the next column. The last carry reaches the final product bit.

The Braun multiplier is the plain unsigned array just described. Row j is A AND b<sub>j</sub>, shifted left by j. Row 0 has no shift. Row 1 is shifted one place, row 2 two places, and so on. Each column adds the bits that land in it plus the carry from the column above. The layout is rectangular and regular, so it maps cleanly to layout and to a cell library.

items: Gate count: n<sup>2</sup> AND gates and n(n−1) full adders for an n×n array. A 4×4 Braun array has 16 AND gates and 12 full adders.
Critical path: the slowest signal enters near the top and travels down the diagonal carry chain, then across the last row. It grows with n, not with n<sup>2</sup>.
No correction terms: every partial product is used exactly as generated. Braun is unsigned only.

blocks.text: A simple delay model is t<sub>p</sub> ≈ (n−1)t<sub>c</sub> + t<sub>last</sub>, where t<sub>c</sub> is the carry delay of one full adder and t<sub>last</sub> is the final carry ripple to the top product bit. This is only a first estimate; wire delay and gate sizing matter in real layout (see Unit 3, delay estimation). Some syllabi ask only for the block diagram and the partial product array, not this estimate.

Signed numbers use two's complement. For an n-bit number, A = −a<sub>n−1</sub>2<sup>n−1</sup> + Σ<sub>i=0</sub><sup>n−2</sup> a<sub>i</sub>2<sup>i</sup>. The top bit has weight −2<sup>n−1</sup>, not +2<sup>n−1</sup>. If you sign-extend both inputs to 2n bits and use a Braun array, the array becomes larger and the sign bits create long rows of copies. Baugh-Wooley keeps the n×n array and corrects the sign inside it.

Generate the low bits normally: a<sub>i</sub>b<sub>j</sub> for i,j ≤ n−2. For a partial product with exactly one sign bit, use the inverted bit: NOT(a<sub>n−1</sub>b<sub>j</sub>) for j ≤ n−2, and NOT(a<sub>i</sub>b<sub>n−1</sub>) for i ≤ n−2. Keep the corner a<sub>n−1</sub>b<sub>n−1</sub> unchanged. Then add two 1 bits at fixed positions: bit n and bit 2n−1. In modulo 2<sup>2n</sup> arithmetic, these two 1s are the correction constant 2<sup>n</sup> + 2<sup>2n−1</sup>.

blocks.where: P<sub>BW</sub> is the signed product modulo 2<sup>2n</sup>; NOT(x) is 1−x; the two added powers are the two 1 bits; all powers of 2 are bit positions in the final product.

blocks.text: Baugh-Wooley needs n<sup>2</sup> AND gates, 2(n−1) inverters for the mixed sign bits, two constant 1 cells, and about n(n−1) full adders. It avoids a separate sign-fix adder and avoids sign extension rows. The array topology and diagonal carry path stay the same as Braun, so the delay is still dominated by the diagonal carry. The saving is area and regularity, not a shorter critical path.

figure.caption: Each row is the multiplicand gated by one multiplier bit; the row for b2 = 0 adds nothing, and the carry path steps diagonally to the last row.

spec.title: 4×4 Braun array, a = 1101
spec.aria: Each row is the multiplicand gated by one bit of the multiplier, and the row gated by b2 equals zero so it adds nothing.

examples.question: Multiply a = 1101₂ (13) by b = 1011₂ (11) on a 4×4 Braun array. Show every partial product row, its place value, the sum, and the final 8-bit product.
steps: Read the multiplier bits from LSB: b0=1, b1=1, b2=0, b3=1.
Row for b0=1: A×1 = 1101₂ = 13. Place value 2^0=1, so contribution 13×1=13.
examples.check:
a = int('1101', 2)
b = int('1011', 2)
rows = []
for j in range(4):
    bit = (b >> j) & 1
    rows.append((a * bit) << j)
print(a)
print(b)
for r in rows:
    print(r)
print(sum(rows))
print(a*b)

traps: In Braun, adding the partial products without their place-value shifts. Row 1 is shifted one place, not added as the same weight as row 0.
In Baugh-Wooley, dropping the two correction 1 bits, or inverting the corner a<sub>n−1</sub>b<sub>n−1</sub>. The corner has a positive weight and stays normal.
Inverting every sign-bit row completely. Only partial products with exactly one sign bit are inverted; the corner is the exception.
Mixing the counts: an n×n array has n<sup>2</sup> AND gates and n(n−1) full adders, not n<sup>2</sup> full adders.
Assuming array delay is n<sup>2</sup> gate delays. The critical path is the diagonal carry plus the final ripple, roughly linear in n.

quiz.q: For an n×n Braun array, how many AND gates and full adders are used?
quiz.a: n² AND gates and n(n−1) full adders. For n=4: 16 AND gates and 12 full adders.

quiz.q: Why do the carries in an array multiplier move diagonally instead of along one row?
quiz.a: Each partial product row is shifted by one column. A carry out of column k in row j has weight 2^(k+1) and must enter column k+1 of the next row. That next row is shifted, so the carry path steps one row down and one column right.

quiz.q: Use a 4×4 Braun array to multiply a = 1010₂ (10) by b = 0110₂ (6). List the four rows and the product.
In Baugh-Wooley, why is the corner partial product a<sub>n−1</sub>b<sub>n−1</sub> not inverted while the other sign-bit partial products are inverted?
quiz.a: The corner term has weight +2^(2n−2) in the signed expansion, because negative times negative is positive. The mixed terms have negative weights. Inverting the mixed AND terms and adding 2^n+2^(2n−1) turns those negatives into valid positive array bits. Inverting the corner would remove the positive term and break the correction.

quiz.q: For a 6×6 Baugh-Wooley multiplier, give n², n(n−1), and the number of mixed sign partial products that are inverted.
quiz.a: n=6: n²=36 AND gates; n(n−1)=30 full adders; mixed sign bits = 2(n−1)=10.

quiz.q: Why does Baugh-Wooley beat sign-extending both inputs and using a Braun array?
quiz.a: Sign extension widens the array and adds rows of repeated sign bits, so more adders and larger area. B-W keeps the n×n array and corrects the sign with inverted mixed terms and two constant 1s. It also avoids a separate sign-fix adder.

quiz.q: Compare the critical paths of Braun and Baugh-Wooley arrays. What is the same and what is different?
quiz.a: Both use the same n×n array of AND gates and full adders, so both have a diagonal carry path through about n rows plus a final ripple. B-W adds inverters in the partial product generation and two constant 1 cells; those add a small fixed delay. The main delay order is still O(n), not O(n²).

quiz.q: What correction bits does an n×n Baugh-Wooley array add?
quiz.a: Two 1 bits, at bit positions n and 2n−1.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real chips rarely use a bare array for wide multiplication; they combine Booth recoding, a Wallace tree, and a fast final adder. The Baugh-Wooley idea still appears inside signed multipliers and in hardware interview questions. Search next for "Baugh-Wooley multiplier array" and "array multiplier critical path".
